steps: Nitrogen is required by plants to make proteins and nucleic acids, and it is also a component of chlorophyll.
Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and is therefore essential for photosynthesis.
Magnesium also activates some enzymes involved in plant metabolism.
items.finalAnswer: Nitrogen is needed to make proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll; magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates enzymes.

steps: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata; guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets from leaf margins through hydathodes.
Transpiration usually takes place mainly during the daytime, while guttation usually occurs at night or in the early morning.
Transpiration is caused by evaporation of water from plant surfaces; guttation occurs when root pressure pushes liquid water out of the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Transpiration is mainly daytime loss of water vapour through stomata, whereas guttation is usually night or early-morning loss of liquid water through hydathodes.

steps: In the light, photosynthesis in guard cells produces sugars from stored starch; the increased sugar concentration lowers the water potential of the guard cells.
Water enters the guard cells from neighbouring cells by osmosis, making them turgid.
Because the inner walls of the guard cells are thicker and less elastic than the outer walls, the turgid guard cells curve apart and the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, sugars in the guard cells are converted back into starch, decreasing their solute concentration.
Water moves out of the guard cells by osmosis, so they become flaccid and the stomatal pore closes.
items.finalAnswer: Light changes starch into sugars in guard cells; water enters by osmosis and the stomata open. In darkness, sugars change back into starch; water leaves by osmosis and the stomata close.

steps: The outermost layer of the root is the epidermis. Its cells may form root hairs, which increase the surface area for absorption.
Inside the epidermis is the cortex, made mainly of thin-walled parenchyma cells; water and dissolved salts pass through it towards the centre of the root.
The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis, which surrounds the vascular tissues.
The vascular tissues are arranged in the central region: xylem conducts water and mineral salts, while phloem conducts food.
Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water.
Mineral salts are absorbed from the soil mainly by active transport through root-hair cells; this may also help water enter by osmosis.
Water and dissolved salts pass across the cortex and endodermis into the xylem, which transports them upwards through the plant.
items.finalAnswer: The root has an epidermis with root hairs, a cortex, an endodermis and central vascular tissues containing xylem and phloem. Root hairs absorb water by osmosis and mineral salts mainly by active transport; these enter the xylem for transport through the plant.

steps: Temperature: As temperature rises, water evaporates more rapidly from the moist surfaces of mesophyll cells and water vapour diffuses out through the stomata faster; therefore, transpiration increases. A fall in temperature slows transpiration.

Wind: Wind removes the moist layer of air surrounding a leaf. This maintains a steep diffusion gradient between the leaf and the outside air, so water vapour diffuses out faster and transpiration increases. Still air allows moisture to collect around the leaf and slows transpiration.

Humidity: Humid air contains more water vapour, reducing the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the outside air; transpiration therefore decreases. Dry air increases this difference and increases transpiration.
items.finalAnswer: Higher temperature and wind generally increase transpiration by speeding evaporation or removing moist air around leaves; high humidity decreases transpiration by reducing the water-vapour diffusion gradient.

steps: Water and mineral salts are absorbed from the soil by root hairs; water enters mainly by osmosis and mineral salts mainly by active transport.
They move through the root cortex and endodermis into the xylem vessels.
Water evaporates from the moist walls of leaf cells and diffuses out through the stomata. This loss of water from leaves is transpiration.

Transpiration creates a pulling force in the xylem. The continuous column of water is pulled upwards from the roots to the leaves; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help maintain the column.
Root pressure may also help push water upwards, especially when transpiration is low.
Mineral salts dissolved in the water are carried with it through the xylem to the leaves and other parts of the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Water and mineral salts enter through root hairs and pass into the xylem. Water loss from leaves creates transpiration pull, drawing the continuous water column and dissolved salts upwards; root pressure may also assist.

steps: Food, mainly sucrose, is produced in the leaves, which are the sources; growing or storage organs that use or store food are the sinks.
At the source, sucrose is actively loaded from leaf cells into the sieve tubes of the phloem.
The increased sugar concentration in the phloem lowers its water potential, so water enters from the neighbouring xylem by osmosis.
The entry of water raises the pressure in the phloem at the source.
At the sink, sucrose is unloaded from the phloem and is used or stored. The sugar concentration and pressure in the phloem there are lower than at the source.
Water moves out of the phloem at the sink, often returning to the xylem. The pressure difference drives the phloem sap from the source to the sink; this is the pressure flow mechanism.
items.finalAnswer: Sucrose is actively loaded into phloem at the source, drawing in water by osmosis and raising pressure. At the sink, sugar is unloaded and water leaves, creating lower pressure; the pressure difference moves food through the phloem from source to sink.
